body_markdown:
We run down 11 great car movies. Are they the best? Greatest of all time? Decide for yourself.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


## *American Graffiti*


One of the most iconic film cars ever, John Milner’s ’32 Ford from American Graffiti. As other characters in the coming-of-age flick move on, the yellow coupe and Milner (played by Paul Le Mat) stay forever young.


Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images


**Released:** 1973


**Directed by:** George Lucas


**Starring:** Ron Howard, Richard Dreyfuss, Paul Le Mat, Charles Martin Smith


So much of the action happens in or around cars in George Lucas’ 1973 nostalgia play about his teenage years in Modesto, California, that the film couldn’t exist without them. The cars are the co-stars in this coming-of-age tale set amid the middle-American cruising culture of one late-summer night in 1962. Lucas, a cruiser and racer himself before suffering a horrific crash on the eve of his high school graduation, made an inspired choice casting a souped-up ’32 Ford and a bitchin’ ’58 Impala as his star cars. They play vital supporting roles to his four protagonists as they shuffle their way toward adulthood, accompanied by a nearly nonstop soundtrack of period doo-wop standards.


Screen Archives/Getty Images


> The cars are the co-stars in this coming-of-age tale set amid the middle-American cruising culture of one late-summer night in 1962.


In film, cars often signify transition for the characters through both space and time. But in[American Graffiti](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/50-years-of-american-graffiti-the-cars-the-music-and-the-everlasting-impact/) , it’s almost the opposite; the cars circle Modesto endlessly as if they are just a chrome-and-tailfin carousel, and it’s up to Steve and Curt and John and Toad to decide when to jump off, if ever. Curt, played by an as-yet-undiscovered Richard Dreyfuss, eventually realizes that both it and the white Thunderbird he has been chasing are illusions, and that it’s time to move on. As Ron Howard’s character Steve says in the opening of the film, “You just can’t stay 17 forever.”


*American Graffiti* was an enormous hit, fully charming a post-Vietnam audience that was perhaps pining for those innocent days of teenage boredom and motorized restlessness fueled by 30-cent gasoline, and it kicked off a decades-long love affair with ’50s cars and culture that is still with us today. Lucas soon departed, quite famously, for a galaxy far, far away, but many of us are very happy to return to Mel’s Diner over and over to sip cherry Cokes and milkshakes, jive to the Wolfman, and keep an eye out for the cops and that badass Chevy. — *Aaron Robinson*


##
*Gone in Sixty Seconds*


In the original Gone in 60 Seconds, one of the greatest (and longest) car chase scenes in film history played out over the suburban Los Angeles streetscapes of the early 1970s, with period dress and grooming to match.


Courtesy H.B. Halicki Mercantile Company


**Released:** 1974


**Directed by:** H.B. Halicki


**Starring:** H.B. Halicki, Marion Busia, Jerry Daugirda, Ronald Halicki


With all due respect to Nicolas Cage and his 2000 remake, we are giving the nod here to H.B. “Toby” Halicki’s original, the car-crash epic to end all car-crash epics. The “plot” of the original *GI60S* is clearly an afterthought. Protagonist Maindrian Pace (played by Halicki himself) is leading two lives: one as a suave and self-assured insurance adjuster and the other as a savvy chop-shop magnate. (Halicki in real life ran an impound/demolition yard.) For no apparent reason, Argentine gangsters make it worth his while to steal 48 high-end cars over the course of five days. Each of the cars on the shopping list is given a woman’s name as a code, lest the cops listen in and find out what’s going on.


One of these cars is, of course, Eleanor, played by a yellow ’71 Mustang SportsRoof visually updated to portray a ’73 Mach 1. There were two Eleanors: the stunt car, which was extensively modified with a full NASCAR roll cage, the transmission welded to the frame, individual rear locking brakes, and a 3-inch-thick steel skid plate on the undercarriage to help it survive the film’s climactic 128-foot jump. The second Eleanor, basically stock and used for interior shots, survives to this day.


Courtesy H.B. Halicki Mercantile Company


The movie was shot, for the most part, without official sanction, often on Sundays when filming permit inspectors were sleeping late and local police enforcement was at a low ebb. Apart from the fact that 93 cars were wrecked or heavily damaged over the course of the filming, it’s worth seeing the movie as a real-life period piece. The cars, both in action and parked, are stock (excluding the stunt Eleanor) and offer a picture of Southern California automotive life a half-century ago.


Courtesy H.B. Halicki Mercantile Company


The vehicular mayhem that Halicki pioneered—the combination of massive crashes, chases, and pileups on the big screen—is now considered an earmark of a film genre unto itself. Even films with scripts written by actual screenwriters like *Smokey and the Bandit, Mad Max, To Live and Die in L.A., Ronin* , and *The Blues Brothers* owe a huge debt to Halicki, now recognized as a man of vision despite his dispensing with narrative norms. — *Bob Merlis, Excerpted from “[50 Years Ago, Gone in 60 Seconds Broke All the Rules—and 93 Cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/fifty-years-ago-gone-in-60-seconds-broke-all-the-rules-and-93-cars/) ”*


##
*Two-Lane Blacktop*


Laurie Bird plays a troubled teenager who tags along on the road trip and racing journey of the Driver (James Taylor, center) and the Mechanic (Dennis Wilson).


Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images


**Released:** 1971


**Directed by:** Monte Hellman


**Starring:** James Taylor, Warren Oates, Laurie Bird, Dennis Wilson


The American counterculture coming-of-age movie was a familiar conceit by 1971. *The Graduate* (1967) and *Easy Rider* (1969) had paved the way both artistically and commercially, leaving director Monte Hellman an opportunity to take the genre down the road of deep car geekdom. His tribute to muscle cars and street racing clearly speaks the language of postwar car culture even as it recognizes that the wider environment is convulsing. The empty spaces of the American Southwest symbolize the loneliness of modern America as a new generation seeks meaning.


*Two-Lane Blacktop* opens at night, on an industrial street in South Los Angeles. A primer gray 1955 Chevy two-door and a red Dodge Charger Hemi edge into position, then peel off. At the wheel of the Chevy—heavily modified with a 454 V-8 and M22 Muncie Rock Crusher four-speed—is the Driver, played by James Taylor. Yes, that James Taylor, flush with youth and fresh off the success of his breakthrough album *Sweet Baby James.* Riding shotgun is Beach Boys drummer Dennis Wilson, playing the Mechanic.


Their mission is clear: roaming state to state to pick street-racing battles and win enough bread to keep driving, eating, drinking, racing. Maybe loving. To keep moving. Hellman filmed his movie sequentially, over the course of an actual road trip from California to North Carolina, allowing his cast of mostly amateur actors to seize on the spare prose of Rudolph Wurlitzer’s script.


At a Route 66 cafe in Arizona, a love interest emerges from a 1949 Diamond T Model 306 ice truck painted with flower power images. “What kind of car is this, anyway?” asks the Girl, played by Laurie Bird, as she climbs into the Chevy and rests her head against the roll bar.


The viewer by this point might reasonably ask, “What kind of flick is this, anyway?” A road-trip movie with a tortured love triangle? Or an American New Wave love triangle with a street-racing subplot? Regardless, the trio is eastbound and down, the desert valleys of Arizona unfolding outside the Chevy’s windows.


A yellow GTO eventually pulls alongside. At a dusty service station, the Driver and the Mechanic face down the Pontiac’s driver, known as GTO, brilliantly played by Warren Oates. The three men spread out a map on a hood, tracing a route to Washington, D.C., in a cross-country race for pink slips. To this peacocking, the Girl says, simply, “You bore me.”


The loquacious GTO, who has a habit of slamming the Pontiac’s brakes and screeching to a sudden halt to pick up any hitchhiker he sees, is not boring. “I’m racing a Chevy,” he enthuses to one of his rides. “Detroit set it up.” Uh huh. If GTO is an amalgam of every carnival barker, vacuum salesman, and con artist in the American canon, he’s also merely desperate for human connection.


He’s not the only one. The so-called race quickly becomes a sort of mutually supportive, two-car rally. The Mechanic fixes a gas leak in the Pontiac’s carburetors. GTO offers drinks from the wet bar in his trunk.


The enigmatic Girl hops from one car to the other, seemingly trying to figure out which one of these men might be able to deliver her to something, somewhere, she hasn’t described and we can only imagine. GTO dreamily talks about taking her to “Miami, Montreal, and Mexico” after the race is over.


“If I’m not grounded pretty soon,” he tells the Girl as she rides shotgun in the Pontiac, “I’m gonna go into orbit.” That’s one statement from GTO that’s easy to believe. — *Joe DeMatio*


## *Smokey and the Bandit*


The Bandit’s (an impressively mustachioed Burt Reynolds) black and gold 1977 Pontiac Trans Am became the real star of the movie—after the film’s release, sales for the model nearly doubled.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


**Released:** 1977


**Directed by:** Hal Needham


**Starring:** Burt Reynolds, Sally Field, Jerry Reed, Jackie Gleason


> *Keep your foot hard on the pedal*
>
>
> *Son, never mind them brakes*
>
>
> *Let it all hang out ’cause we’ve got a run to make*
>
>
> *The boys are thirsty in Atlanta*
>
>
> *And there’s beer in Texarkana*
>
>
> *And we’ll bring it back no matter what it takes*


In the summer of 1977, a black and gold Pontiac Trans Am, adorned with a screaming chicken on the hood, blasted onto movie screens with Burt Reynolds and his iconic mustache behind the wheel. Smokey and the Bandit, directed by stuntman-turned-filmmaker Hal Needham, is a 1.5-hour car chase that stops only briefly to collect a runaway bride, played by Sally Field. But the Trans Am is the real star—Needham cast it as a key character after seeing a single advertisement for the soon-to-be-released ’77 model.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


Needham and Reynolds were old friends long before cameras rolled. Reynolds championed the project at Universal so his buddy could make his directorial debut, even though he told Needham it was the worst script he’d ever read. Needham, a former Hollywood stuntman with a flair for on-screen action, stretched a $4.3 million budget across the rural Georgia roads standing in for Texarkana. With high-speed driving as the only real plot, most of the dialogue was simply improvised along the way. The two went on to make *Hooper* (1978) and *The Cannonball Run* (1981) together, but *Smokey and the Bandit* is where their collaboration really came alive.


> It was freedom and rebellion with a V-8 engine, and that was exactly what America wanted to see.


CB radios and 18-wheelers were already hugely popular in 1977, and Needham fed both into the mix here. Jerry Reed, as trucker Cledus Snow, delivered the film’s iconic theme, “East Bound and Down”—a song so perfectly suited to the open road that the director reportedly said he’d “choke him” if he changed a single word.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


But the Trans Am delivered the film’s most iconic moment: a jump over a missing bridge, with Jackie Gleason’s hilariously outmatched Sheriff Buford T. Justice in hot pursuit. Landing the escape was Reynolds, cowboy hat dipped low, breaking the fourth wall with that famous laugh—as if he and the audience were in on the same unbelievable joke.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


The Bandit’s Trans Am transcends mere transportation. It was freedom and rebellion with a V-8 engine, and in 1977, that was exactly what America wanted to see on the silver screen. — *Todd Kraemer*

## *Mad Max*


From family man to stone-cold killer, Mel Gibson’s Mad Max is the story of a cop’s descent into darkness as the world collapses with him. The black Interceptor, a ’73 Ford Falcon, becomes his personal Angel of Death.


Courtesy Everett Collection


**Released:** 1979


**Directed by:** George Miller


**Starring:** Mel Gibson, Hugh Keays-Byrne, Joanne Samuel, Steve Bisley


Between the pounding score, the quick glimpses of a crumbling Hall of Justice and a debris-littered road, and a cop salaciously spying on two naked canoodlers, less than a minute of *Mad Max* has lapsed before you know the world that you’re entering is thoroughly bent. George Miller and Byron Kennedy’s original 1979 masterpiece is one tight work of indie filmmaking; there isn’t a wasted frame in the 93 sizzling minutes to follow. As we have learned ad nauseam from superhero movies, origin stories are often the best films within a franchise, and *Mad Max* is no exception.


What makes the original *Max* stand apart from the postapocalyptic blockbusters that followed—besides the low-budget graininess and bandit style to its cinematography—is the nervous uncertainty of the setting. In the film, society as we know it, with bureaucrats and courts and policemen in uniforms, is still functioning, if fractured. A world on a knife’s edge is, particularly in our own time, far more interesting than one that has already tipped into chaos, with all the predictable clichés of nihilistic cruelty and violence that follow. With the original Max, you’re left to wonder who the good guys are and if there are indeed consequences for any of it. “You’re really gonna get it this time,” bleats one of the cops after his partner rams a van during the opening calamitous chase. “He had his indicator on!” Nobody worries about turn indicators after the bomb drops.


The first 10 minutes of this low-budget indie thriller leave you breathless. Shot in real time with no special effects, it somehow seems way more exciting than today’s digital offerings.


Courtesy Everett Collection


In *Mad Max* , the law wears black and delights in carnage, while the leaders of the biker gang are erudite and highly philosophical, spouting poetry on the fly. Max is a dedicated family man, but also the most ruthless cop on the force. None of it is predictable, which makes it riveting. These subtle story nuances get increasingly lost in the big-budget crash-fests that come after, as dazzling as they are. And, let’s face it, the action in the original *Max* is one of a kind, the actors and stuntpeople shot at actual speed by fearless, helmetless camerapeople strapped to fenders and astride motorcycle back seats, all seemingly lacking any self-preservation instincts. You just can’t get this intensity with computer cartoons—not yet, anyway.


The cars (and bikes) in *Mad Max* are vital to the story. As Mel Gibson’s Max slips from the light into the darkness, a metaphor for the collapsing world around him, he abandons his gaily colored yellow patrol car for the black Interceptor. The car is his murderous partner going forward, effectively becoming the Angel of Death. Or, as one of the bikers says prophetically at the beginning, “the mighty hand of vengeance, sent down to smite the un-roadworthy.” Having made his bloody bargain, Max is doomed to spend the next three movies seeking redemption in increasingly bizarre and outlandish spectacles. Meanwhile, his avenging car, the “last of the V-8 Interceptors, a piece of history,” sacrifices itself to save Max early in the series’ next (and next best) installment, *The Road Warrior* . All of which makes it one cop and one cop car that we will never forget, even as the rest of it is easily forgotten. — *Aaron Robinson*


## *C’était un Rendez-Vous*


French director Claude Lelouch terrorized the streets of Paris in his Mercedes 450 SEL for 8 minutes, 39 seconds and filmed it all. Watch out, pigeons!


Courtesy Spirit Level Film


**Released:** 1976


**Directed by:** Claude Lelouch


**Starring:** Claude Lelouch, Gunilla Friden


The words flash across the screen: “The film you are about to see was made without any special effects or speed manipulation.” The words fade, followed by the sound of a beating heart. As the scream of an engine reverberates against concrete walls, we realize we are rocketing out of a tunnel onto the streets and that we are in Paris. What follows is an unhinged vehicular attack on the streets of the City of Light, viewed from the nose of an unseen car.


The route takes us up the Avenue Foch and past the famous landmarks of the city, including the Arc de Triomphe, the Luxor Obelisk, and the Louvre. The tires squeal over the cobblestones, and the driver shifts maniacally up and down the gears. What is that exhaust note? It’s a Ferrari V-12, isn’t it? This driver is insane, blasting through red lights, driving up on the sidewalk, and almost colliding with a city bus. Hey, he almost hit that woman walking her dog! What the heck is he doing? Then with a final series of beautifully blipped downshifts, we pass the Sacré-Coeur de Montmartre. The brakes screech and as we come to a stop at the curb, we have our answer: A woman runs up the stairs and out jumps the driver to embrace her. The church bells ring, we see the words “It was a date” and the credit “Filmed by Claude Lelouch.” Distance traveled: 6.5 miles. Red lights blown: 18. Pigeons maimed/killed: 0 (hopefully). Time elapsed: 8 minutes, 39 seconds. For decades, that is all anyone knew about *Rendezvous* .


Rumors circulated that Formula 1 driver Jean-Pierre Beltoise performed the stunt in a Matra Le Mans sports prototype. Another held it was Jacques Laffite in a Ferrari 275 GTB. A cottage industry of sorts sprang up to solve the mystery, analyzing every frame as if it were the Zapruder film. Slowly, over the years, the layers of truth revealed themselves. In 1976, Lelouch had finished shooting a film and had roughly 9 minutes of footage left over. His inspiration came from a personal experience he’d had when he was running late for an appointment and drove across Paris like a madman to be on time.


City officials refused to close the necessary streets for Lelouch to film his fantasy, so he decided to do it without permission. He reduced the risks by shooting at 5:30 a.m. on a Sunday in August, when virtually all of Paris was shut down for vacation. He mounted a gyrostabilized camera to the front of the car, which was his personal Mercedes-Benz 450 SEL 6.9; a fantastic car, but not a Ferrari. The Benz’s self-leveling suspension worked in tandem with the gyrostabilized camera to steady the filming. Since the Benz’s engine sounds were on the sedate side, Lelouch later dubbed in those of a Ferrari 275 GTB. The syncing of the action with the audio is quite good, especially considering the analog tools available at the time.


Later, he confessed to being the driver and that he was arrested for his exploits. “The chief of police called me in,” recalled Lelouch. “He read me a list of all the offenses I’d committed. When he finished, he gave me a black look and asked for my license. He contemplated it for a few moments, then gave it back with a large smile on his face. He said, ‘I promised I would take your license, but I didn’t say for how long.’ I was stupefied. It was a symbolic punishment. Then he added, ‘My children love your little film.’” — *Kirk Seaman*


## *Cars*


Lightning McQueen (Owen Wilson) and a star-studded cast of cameos—celebrity and automotive—helped introduce a new generation to the magic of automobiles.


Courtesy Walt Disney PicturesPixar Animation Studios


**Released:** 2006


**Directed by:** John Lasseter


**Starring:** Owen Wilson, Paul Newman, Bonnie Hunt, Michael Keaton


Earlier this year, NASCAR released a promotional YouTube video in which some of its younger drivers ([Connor Zilisch](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/connor-zilisch-is-nascars-hope-for-the-future/) , 19 at the time, was the youngest; Joey Logano was the oldest at 36) were blindfolded and asked to identify die-cast cars. Most struggled to identify miniatures of a late-model Chevrolet Corvette, a ’67 El Camino, and a fifth-generation Toyota Supra. However, when presented with Lightning McQueen, the arrogant rookie racer and main character of Pixar’s 2006 animated feature *Cars* , all of the drivers instantly identified the anthropomorphic stock car. Admittedly, the NASCAR drivers represent a small sample size, but Cars absolutely made an impression on recent generations of automotive aficionados.


Watch the intro sequence and you’ll understand the appeal. The movie starts in darkness, with Lightning (voiced by Owen Wilson) doing sports psychology visualization exercises: “Speed. I am speed.” He then emerges from his race trailer, light slowly shining on him to reveal a red stock car. Quick cuts of superspeedway racing, MTV style, follow, with howling V-8s and Sheryl Crow’s “Real Gone” soundtracking the sequence. Slow down, you’re gonna crash. I was 11 when I first saw it, and I was hooked.


Pixar was at the height of its powers in 2006—every movie it had released— *Toy Story, Finding Nemo* —was a box-office smash. The animation studio’s formula for making movies sticky to both adults and kids is simple but effective: Mix bang-zoom computer animation and star-studded voice talent with relatable characters who are on emotional journeys. *Cars* is no exception, although the strange implications of the *Cars* universe—a car’s anatomy seems to be an unholy amalgamation of flesh and steel—are left unaddressed.


But what makes *Cars* brilliant is how it cleverly weaves in so many parts of American car culture. The film’s inciting incident is caused by a gang of *Fast & Furious* –style tuner cars, and Lightning ends up stuck in the fictitious Radiator Springs, evoking the many Route 66 towns that were bypassed by the interstate. The flick also does a surprisingly good job of retelling NASCAR history, ranging from the Fabulous Hudson Hornet (voiced by Paul Newman in one of his last feature films) to the blue Plymouth Superbird (voiced by all-time great Richard Petty). The voices of racing legends like Dale Earnhardt Jr., Darrell Waltrip, Michael Schumacher, and Mario Andretti also make cameos.


Even though *Cars* is old enough to legally drive, the opening sequence still gets this 31-year-old author hyped up. Perhaps it’s because *Cars* landed at the perfect time to straddle two generations, or maybe because no one else has tried, but there really hasn’t been a better entry point to turn a car-curious kid into a lifelong enthusiast. — *Chris Stark*


## *The Fast and the Furious*


Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel) and Brian O’Conner (Paul Walker) put modern classics through their paces—with clearly realistic NOS action—on the streets of L.A. in this grounded first entry of the now-fanciful franchise.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


**Released:** 2001


**Directed by:** Rob Cohen


**Starring:** Paul Walker, Vin Diesel, Michelle Rodriguez, Jordana Brewster


This is an odd thing to say about a series best known for its fakery, but the secret to the success and enduring appeal of *The Fast and the Furious* —and here I’m really talking about the 2001 movie, not so much the blockbuster franchise currently going on its dozenth installment—is its authenticity.


I don’t necessarily mean the cars or street races, the details of which entire corners of the internet have devoted themselves to debunking. (No, nitrous doesn’t work like that.) Nor does the plot win many points for realism. It should be noted the first film was inspired by real reporting—a 1998 story by Kenneth Li that appeared in *Vibe* —and is far easier to follow than its increasingly unintelligible successors. Still, it’s clear from the first few frames that you’re not getting a gritty docudrama.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


Courtesy Universal Pictures


> The beating heart of the first film in the blockbuster franchise is in its love of cars and driving, and that feels totally genuine.


Yet the beating heart of the film is love for cars and driving, and that feels totally genuine. There are indulgent shots of cars; not just hot stuff like[Toyota Supras](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/auctions/the-7-most-expensive-fast-furious-movie-cars-ever-sold/) and Dodge Chargers but also workaday Honda Civics modded within an inch of their lives. There’s the exuberant talk of NOS bottles and turbos and “double clutching,” which, even in its silliness, sounded very much like the car-obsessed chatter that consumed my teenage friends and me at the time. Or maybe we sounded like them. We millennials learned facts about cars from all over—magazines, early web forums, *Top Gear* —but this movie gave us a shared language and style.


Millennials came to know and appreciate cars like the 1995 Mitsubishi Eclipse RS, thanks to their appearance in the movie.


Courtesy Universal Pictures


And of course there’s its star, Paul Walker. He became famous (and then, sadly, infamous) for being a true-blue car enthusiast, and that shines through. He not only drives fast, but with apparent relish. When Walker climbs out of his smoking Mitsubishi Eclipse in an early scene, having just lost a race to co-star Vin Diesel, he’s not grimacing or affecting cool-guy detachment. He’s beaming. He tells Diesel, “Dude, I almost had you!” He definitely had us. — *David Zenlea*


## *Chitty Chitty Bang Bang*


There were six different versions of Chitty made for the film, all by Alan Mann Racing in England. AMR was part of Ford’s international motorsports program, working on the GT40 and the Daytona Cobra coupe.


Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images


**Released:** 1968


**Directed by:** Ken Hughes


**Starring:** Dick Van Dyke, Sally Ann Howes, Lionel Jeffries, Gert Fröbe


From the moment the opening credits of *[Chitty Chitty Bang Bang](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/chitty-and-me/)* flashed across the screen of our family’s television in November 1974, I was smitten. First, it starred my favorite actor, Dick Van Dyke. He played the zany Caractacus Potts, father to towheaded twins Jeremy and Jemima. I identified immediately with the children, making it easy for me to imagine myself right alongside them for their adventures dashing across the gorgeous countryside of Edwardian England. The catchy tunes they sing along the way further engaged my fertile imagination.


Then there was Chitty, a glorious fusion of metal and wood and leather. The gleaming aluminum hood polished to a mirror shine. The rich, varnished wood of the boattail body. The luscious lipstick-red leather seats. All of it dazzled and enthralled me. To this day, I’m a sucker for red interiors, as witnessed by my 1976 Cadillac Eldorado convertible.


The movie, which debuted in December 1968, is loosely based on the book of the same name, written by Ian Fleming of James Bond fame. Fleming put in writing the bedtime stories he had been telling his son, Caspar. The name came from a series of cars, each named Chitty Bang Bang, raced in the 1920s by the renowned playboy Count Louis Zborowski. Fleming had seen the cars as a boy, raced at Brooklands in England.


The movie revolves around Jeremy and Jemima finding a wrecked race car in a junkyard. The kindly owner allows the kids to play in the car, imagining themselves reliving its racing exploits. When the children learn the car is about to be sent to the crusher, they convince their father—an eccentric inventor—to buy the car and restore it to its former glory. Chitty’s license plate, GEN11, hints at the car’s magical powers (“genie,” get it?). Not only was Chitty self-driving, but it was also self-flying *and* self-motorboating. That magic has stayed with me over the passing five decades. Even now, there’s a part of me that believes a gentle tug on the steering wheel can send my car—and my imagination—soaring. — *Kirk Seaman*


## *Talladega Nights: The Ballad of Ricky Bobby*


Shake and bake! Will Ferrell’s Ricky Bobby poked good-natured fun at the mid-aughts NASCAR boom—and taught us that if you ain’t first, you’re last.


Courtesy Columbia Pictures/Sony Pictures


**Released:** 2006


**Directed by:** Adam McKay


**Starring:** Will Ferrell, John C. Reilly, Sacha Baron Cohen


Attend any NASCAR race, and you’ll likely overhear multiple one-liners and spot references to *Talladega Nights.* Despite hitting theater screens 20 years ago, the movie remains part of stock car pop culture, especially when the tour stops at its namesake raceway in central Alabama (where you’ll spot at least one fan dressed up as protagonist Ricky Bobby). Rightfully so. The 108-minute movie is densely packed with hilarious dialogue, slapstick comedy, and witty commentary on a sport that’s inherently ridiculous. *This sticker is dangerous and inconvenient, but I do love Fig Newtons.*


Lighthearted as it was, *Talladega* was the product of seriously brilliant comedic minds. Hot off the success of *Anchorman* in 2004, *Saturday Night Live* expats Adam McKay and Will Ferrell set their sights on NASCAR as the arena for their next comedy. In that moment, Ferrell was the funniest guy in Hollywood and stock car racing was the fastest-growing sport in America, ripe for a race to the box office. Of course, it wasn’t the first time the Southern sport was lampooned: Burt Reynolds’ *Stroker Ace* did that in 1983. Nor was it the first time NASCAR was a silver screen smash hit— *Days of Thunder* pulled in $157.9 million at the box office back in 1990. *Help me, Tom Cruise!* But neither of those efforts had the duo of Ferrell and McKay, who co-wrote the film and who followed up *Talladega Nights* with the even funnier *Step Brothers* .


If by some unlikely chance you haven’t seen *Talladega* , the film follows goofball stock car driver Ricky Bobby, portrayed by Ferrell, through a series of peaks and valleys in his NASCAR career. Ricky Bobby is often the butt of the joke, playing a simpleton obsessed with speed. Ferrell is joined by an all-star cast of actors from Sacha Baron Cohen to Amy Adams and a healthy dose of cameos by actual NASCAR drivers. Ferrell’s magical on-screen chemistry with John C. Reilly, who plays Ricky Bobby’s best friend and teammate Cal Naughton Jr., anchors the film, and the duo provide some of the best laughs.


Over the past two decades, *Talladega Nights* cemented itself in the zeitgeist not just as a successful big-budget comedy, the kind that doesn’t get made anymore, but as a perennially appealing sendup of NASCAR culture. That it’s still heavily quoted two decades on proves that this potent symbol of middle America can look at itself and laugh. — *Cameron Neveu*


## *Steve McQueen: The Man & Le Mans*


Steve McQueen’s labor of love, *Le Mans* , might have lacked plot and character development, but it featured real-deal race cars strapped with cameras.


Courtesy FilmRise


**Released:** 2015


**Directed by:** Gabriel Clarke and John McKenna


**Starring:** Steve McQueen, Neile Adams, Chad McQueen, Derek Bell


*Steve McQueen: The Man & Le Mans* is a great documentary about a bad movie. That movie, *Le Mans* , was McQueen’s 1971 passion project. Hot off hits like *Bullitt* and *The Thomas Crown Affair* , McQueen had “the juice,” as they say in Hollywood. Studios lined up to fund his next project, a love letter to endurance racing.


For *Le Mans* , McQueen wanted to put the audience behind the wheel of a race car to feel the things drivers feel: the rush of the speed and the uncanny umbilical cord that grows between human and machine. “We had the star; we had the drivers,” *The Man & Le Mans* consulting producer Hal Hamilton recalled. “We had an incredible array of technical support; we had everything.” What they didn’t have was a script.


During the 1970 24 Hours of Le Mans race, and for months after, McQueen’s crew filmed a squad of professional drivers behind the wheels of legit race cars like the Porsche 917 and the Ferrari 512. McQueen’s demands for strict authenticity meant shooting at triple-digit speeds over multiple takes.


The directors and writers sent to France to wrangle a story that a mass-market audience would pay to see were all thwarted by McQueen’s vision. The central tension of the documentary is that McQueen imagined a film far different from the one the studio, Cinema Center Films, thought it was buying. The eventual film has the best period racing footage available but alas, no story to be found. It was a commercial failure.


Forty-four years later, directors Gabriel Clarke and John McKenna used previously unseen footage and period McQueen interviews to tell the harrowing tale of the war that developed between McQueen and the rotating cast of writers, directors, and handlers brought in to rein him in. They largely failed, as many of them described, wistfully, decades later in interviews conducted by Clarke and McKenna.


The documentary is a fascinating and insightful portrait of an artist struggling with a singular concept that he’s unable to translate to reality. McQueen had a deep and abiding passion for racing that he wanted to communicate. But he needed others to help him get there, and he couldn’t get them to see and feel what he did. His frustration led to all sorts of naughty on-set behavior and production calamities. One driver lost a leg in an accident. Careers were derailed or destroyed. As Clarke and McKenna deftly demonstrate, it turns out that producing a movie with no story makes for one helluva compelling tale. — *Larry Webster*
